```{r setup}
library(simplelm)
```

## Fit a model with one predictor

Add horsepower (`hp`) to the model along with vehicle weight (`wt`).
The coefficient for each predictor estimates the change in fuel economy
associated with a one-unit increase in that predictor, holding the other
predictor fixed.

```{r multiple-predictor}
multi_formula <- mpg ~ wt + hp + qsec + am
fit_multiple <- matrix_lm(multi_formula, data = mtcars)
fit_multiple$coefficients
```

## Reconstruct the design matrix

The design matrix contains an intercept column and one column for each
predictor. Multiplying the returned `Q` and `R` matrices reconstructs
the design matrix. The comparison below should return `TRUE`.

```{r reconstruct-design}
X <- model.matrix(multi_formula, data = mtcars)
X_reconstructed <- fit_multiple$Q %*% fit_multiple$R

# Check dimensions first, then compare the numerical entries.
stopifnot(identical(dim(X), dim(X_reconstructed)))
all.equal(X, X_reconstructed, check.attributes = FALSE)
```

## Compare observed and fitted fuel economy

Multiply the reconstructed design matrix by the estimated coefficients
to calculate fitted MPG for the cars in `mtcars`. Each point represents
one car. Points on the dashed line have equal observed and fitted MPG.

```{r observed-vs-fitted, fig.width=6, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Observed and fitted fuel economy for the cars in mtcars."}
observed_mpg <- mtcars$mpg
fitted_mpg <- drop(X_reconstructed %*% fit_multiple$coefficients)
mpg_range <- range(observed_mpg, fitted_mpg)

plot(
  observed_mpg, fitted_mpg,
  xlim = mpg_range, ylim = mpg_range, asp = 1,
  xlab = "Observed fuel economy (MPG)",
  ylab = "Fitted fuel economy (MPG)",
  pch = 19, col = "steelblue"
)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "gray40")
```

## Comparison with R's lm()

```{r compare results with stats:lm package}
base_fit <- stats::lm(multi_formula, data = mtcars)

all.equal(fit_multiple$coefficients, coef(base_fit))
all.equal(fitted_mpg, unname(fitted(base_fit)))

```

```{r benchmark}
set.seed(625)

time_fit <- function(fit_model, repetitions = 30L) {
  elapsed <- replicate(5L, {
    system.time({
      for (i in seq_len(repetitions)) fit_model()
    })[["elapsed"]]
  })

  1000 * median(elapsed) / repetitions
}

compare_speed <- function(n) {
  dat <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = rnorm(n))
  dat$y <- 1 + 2 * dat$x1 - dat$x2 + 0.5 * dat$x3 + rnorm(n)
  form <- y ~ x1 + x2 + x3

  data.frame(
    n = n,
    matrix_lm_ms = time_fit(function() matrix_lm(form, data = dat)),
    lm_ms = time_fit(function() stats::lm(form, data = dat))
  )
}

rbind(compare_speed(1000), compare_speed(10000))

```
On the simulated full-rank datasets, matrix_lm() and stats::lm() produced coefficient estimates that agreed within numerical tolerance. stats::lm() took less time per fit at both sample sizes. matrix_lm() returns Q and R explicitly so users can inspect how the least squares estimates are computed.
